The kingdom advances through self-sacrifice, not coercion. Through persuasion, not legislation. Through the slow, patient work of communities living out an alternative vision of human flourishing.

When the church aligns itself with a political party, it inevitably subordinates kingdom ethics to partisan strategy. It must excuse the sins of its allies and exaggerate the sins of its opponents. It must treat electoral victory as evidence of divine favor and electoral defeat as evidence of spiritual warfare. It must, in short, adopt the logic of the political world, a logic of power, competition, and zero-sum calculation, and baptize it in the language of faith.

This is precisely what the prophets condemned. When Amos thundered against Israel, he was not addressing a secular state. He was addressing a religious society that had confused its own prosperity with God's approval. When Jeremiah wept over Jerusalem, he wept over a people who had placed their trust in political alliances and military power rather than in the justice and mercy of God. The prophetic tradition does not reject political engagement. It rejects the idolatry of political power, the belief that the right legislation, the right president, the right Supreme Court can accomplish what only the Spirit of God can accomplish.

> "The church that marries the spirit of the age will find itself widowed in the next." This aphorism, often attributed to Dean Inge, describes precisely what has happened to American evangelicalism's political project. The movement married itself to the Republican Party, and as the party's character has changed, the church has found itself bound to positions and personalities that contradict its own stated values.

## The Global Perspective

The American fusion of evangelical Christianity with right-wing politics is not universal. It is, in fact, an anomaly. In most of the world, politically engaged Christianity looks very different.

In Latin America, the most significant political theology of the twentieth century was liberation theology, a movement that read the Gospel through the lens of the poor and the oppressed and argued that God's preferential option was for those at the bottom of the social hierarchy. Whatever one thinks of liberation theology's Marxist analytical framework, its central claim, that the God of the Bible is not neutral in the face of injustice, is difficult to dismiss on scriptural grounds. Gustavo Gutierrez, Leonardo Boff, and Oscar Romero articulated a vision of political Christianity that was radical, justice-oriented, and rooted in the lived experience of the poor.

In South Africa, the church played a central role in the anti-apartheid movement. Desmond Tutu, Allan Boesak, and Beyers Naude drew on the prophetic tradition to challenge a system of racial oppression that was itself justified by a theological framework, the Dutch Reformed Church's theology of separate development. The Kairos Document of 1985, produced by South African theologians, distinguished between "state theology" (which legitimized the status quo), "church theology" (which offered vague appeals to reconciliation without addressing structural injustice), and "prophetic theology" (which named the sin and demanded concrete change). This taxonomy remains remarkably useful.

In South Korea, the minjung theology movement connected Christian faith with the struggles of workers, students, and democracy activists under authoritarian rule. In the Philippines, the church was instrumental in the People Power Revolution of 1986. In Poland, Catholic social teaching provided the intellectual framework for the Solidarity movement. In each case, political Christianity was oriented toward justice, liberation, and the empowerment of the oppressed, not toward the consolidation of power by those who already possessed it.

The American model, in which Christianity functions as the spiritual legitimation of an existing power structure, is the exception, not the rule. This should give American Christians pause.

## How to Be Engaged Without Being Captured

None of this means Christians should withdraw from political life. The apolitical fundamentalism of the early twentieth century was its own form of failure, a refusal to love one's neighbor in the public square. The question is not whether Christians should be politically engaged but how they can be engaged without being captured by partisan loyalties that distort their witness.

Several principles emerge from the wreckage of the Religious Right. First, the church must maintain its prophetic independence from every party and every politician. This means the church must be willing to critique its allies as readily as its opponents. A church that speaks only against the sins of the other party is not prophetic. It is partisan with a stained-glass veneer.

Second, Christians must resist the reduction of their ethical tradition to a handful of issues selected for partisan convenience. The full range of biblical ethics, including economic justice, peacemaking, care for creation, hospitality to the stranger, and the dignity of every human being, must inform political engagement. A "whole-life" ethic, as articulated by figures like Ron Sider and the late Cardinal Joseph Bernardin, refuses to let any party claim a monopoly on Christian values.

Third, the church must recover the distinction between penultimate and ultimate loyalties. Political engagement is penultimate, important but not final. The kingdom of God is ultimate. When penultimate loyalties displace ultimate ones, when the party becomes the church, when the president becomes the pastor, when the platform becomes the creed, idolatry has occurred, regardless of how sincerely the participants believe otherwise.

Fourth, the church must learn from the global church. The American evangelical fusion of faith and right-wing politics is not the only model available. Christians in other contexts have demonstrated that it is possible to be politically engaged, passionately committed to justice, and theologically serious without becoming the chaplains of any political movement.

Finally, the church must recover its eschatological patience. The kingdom of God will not arrive through an election. It will not be established by a Supreme Court ruling. It will not be advanced by controlling school boards or winning culture wars. The kingdom comes as it has always come: through the slow, faithful, often invisible work of communities that embody an alternative way of being human. This does not mean politics is unimportant. It means politics is not ultimate. And when the church forgets that distinction, it loses not only its prophetic voice but its very identity.

The story of the Religious Right is a cautionary tale, not a model to be emulated. The church entered politics seeking to change the world and discovered that the world had changed the church. The path forward requires not less engagement but a fundamentally different kind, one rooted in the full breadth of the biblical tradition, accountable to the global church, and freed from the illusion that any political arrangement can substitute for the kingdom of God.

chapters.title: Whose Kingdom? Jesus and Political Power
chapters.summary: Jesus was offered every kingdom of the world by someone who actually had them to give, and what he did with the offer settles the question we keep reopening.
chapters.body:
Before Jesus preached a sermon or healed a single body, he was taken to a high place and shown every kingdom of the world. The one showing him had the authority to make the offer. All these I will give you, he said, if you will fall down and worship me (Matthew 4:9 ESV). It was not a hollow temptation. The kingdoms were really on the table. And the price was a single act of worship aimed in the wrong direction. Jesus refused, and the refusal is the founding decision of his entire ministry. He would not take the kingdoms of the world on the terms by which the kingdoms of the world are taken.

We reopen this question every election cycle as though Jesus never settled it. We ask how the church should hold political power, what it should do with influence, how it should bend the levers of the state toward righteousness. These are not foolish questions. But they are downstream of a prior question that the wilderness already answered, and we keep skipping the answer because we do not like it. The prior question is whether the kingdom of God advances by the means the world uses to advance its kingdoms. Jesus said no in the desert, said it again to Pilate, and said it most loudly on a cross. We have spent two thousand years pretending we did not hear.

The strongest objection to a hands-off reading deserves a full hearing, because it is not the objection of cowards. It comes from believers who say the church cannot retreat from public life and call the retreat holiness. They point out that the prophets confronted kings, that John the Baptist lost his head for telling Herod his marriage was unlawful, that William Wilberforce used political power to end the British slave trade, that Bonhoeffer joined a plot against Hitler. They say that to abandon the public square in the name of a kingdom not of this world is to leave the vulnerable at the mercy of whoever does not abandon it. That is a serious charge, and it is largely true. A church that washes its hands of power has often washed its hands of the people that power crushes.

I want to grant the whole of it, because the half-grant is a cheat. The prophets did confront kings. Christians did and should engage the machinery of justice. A faith that has nothing to say to Pharaoh is not the faith of the Exodus. The error I am warning against is not engagement. It is the belief that engagement means seizing the throne, that the kingdom of God is the kind of kingdom you install by winning, that Christ needs to govern through Caesar because he cannot govern any other way. Wilberforce did not try to make Britain the kingdom of God. He pressed a particular evil with the tools at hand and trusted a Lord who reigns whether or not the vote goes his way. The difference between that and Christian nationalism is the difference between salt and a coup.

So carry the governing text to its end. When Jesus stood before Pilate, the only man in the room with the power to kill him, Pilate asked if he was a king. Jesus answered with the sentence that should have ended the argument forever. My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over (John 18:36 ESV). Read what he is saying. He is not saying his kingdom has no bearing on this world. He is saying it does not come from this world's source and does not advance by this world's method. The proof he offers is the absence of fighting. A kingdom that fights to install its king is a kingdom of this world by definition. The kingdom of God is recognizable precisely by its refusal to take up the sword that every earthly kingdom requires.

This is the reversal that the nationalist reading cannot survive. The crowd on Palm Sunday wanted exactly the king the tempter offered, a king who would ride into Jerusalem and throw out Rome and restore the throne of David by force. They spread their cloaks and shouted hosanna, which means save us, and they meant save us from the empire. Jesus rode in on a donkey, the animal of peace, not a warhorse, and within the week the same crowd was screaming for his blood, because he would not be the king they wanted. They wanted power that conquers. He gave them power that dies. The triumphal entry is a deliberate refusal of the political kingship the people demanded, and we have turned it into a parade, missing that it was a protest against everything we use it to celebrate.

Augustine watched a Christian empire convince itself it was the kingdom of God, and he wrote the book that should have inoculated us. There are two cities, he said, built by two loves, and they are mixed together in this age so that no earthly city is the city of God and none is wholly outside it (Augustine 426). Rome was not the kingdom of God when it was pagan and did not become the kingdom of God when it was Christian. The two cities run through every nation and every heart, and the fatal mistake of every age is to identify one earthly kingdom as the city of God and then to defend that kingdom as though defending God. America is not the city of God. No nation is. The believer holds dual citizenship and knows which passport is eternal.

Stanley Hauerwas pressed this into the bone for our own time. The church does not have a social strategy, he wrote with William Willimon. The church is a social strategy (Hauerwas and Willimon 1989). The way the church holds power is by being a different kind of power, a community that tells the truth, welcomes the stranger, forgives the enemy, and refuses to win by the means that require it to stop being the church. The moment the church decides it must capture the state to accomplish its mission, it has confessed that it no longer believes its own gospel can accomplish anything, that it needs Caesar's sword because the cross was not enough. That confession is the heart of the thing, and it is a confession of unbelief dressed up as zeal.

I have to indict myself here, because I have wanted the shortcut. I have stood in election seasons and felt the pull to believe that if my side simply won, the kingdom would advance, that righteousness was one majority away. That is the wilderness temptation in a voting booth. It offers the kingdoms of the world for a single act of misdirected worship, the worship that says power saves. I have bowed toward it more than once, not with my words but with my anxieties, with where my hope went when the returns came in. The gauge of my hope on election night has told me the truth about which kingdom I was actually serving, and the truth has not always flattered me.

The cross does the decisive work. Because on the cross Jesus took the throne by the one means no empire understands. He did not seize power. He absorbed it. He let the combined authority of temple and empire do its worst, and he forgave them from inside the execution, and on the third day God overturned their verdict. That is how the kingdom comes. Not by climbing the high place and accepting the kingdoms on the tempter's terms, but by going down to the lowest place and being raised by a power no kingdom can kill. The church that grasps for political power has not understood the cross. It is trying to win a war that was already won by losing.

Whose kingdom. Not ours, and not our country's. His. And his does not need our majorities to arrive. It needs our faithfulness while we wait. The shortcut was offered once to a better man than any of us, in a high place, by someone who had the kingdoms to give. He said no, and his no is the pattern. We say yes, again and again, and call our yes obedience.

The kingdom is not of this world. He told us plainly. We keep voting otherwise.
